item.title: [Research] Unlocking BitLocker: Finding Vulnerabilities Without Breaking Encryption - Part 2 (EN)
item.content:encoded:
Part 1: https://hackyboiz.github.io/2026/01/22/banda/BitLocker_part1/ko/

0. Overview

Hello! This is banda from the Dongsangimong team. It has been a little while, but do you remember my BitLocker research post? After taking a break from it for some serious cultivation, I decided to dig into BitLocker again.

In Part 1, we looked at the properties of XTS-AES used by BitLocker and CrashXTS, a mechanism that causes system operations to fail by taking advantage of the lack of ciphertext integrity. In CrashXTS, an attacker cannot write chosen plaintext to an encrypted disk. Instead, they can modify a particular ciphertext block and corrupt its corresponding plaintext block unpredictably.

Directly breaking AES-encrypted data is extremely difficult, so this time let us focus not on the cryptographic algorithm but on how keys are unlocked and used. In this long-awaited return, we will look at interesting vulnerabilities arising from the trust relationship between WinRE and Boot Manager.

1. Why did WinRE become part of BitLocker’s attack surface?

If you have used BitLocker before, this screen will probably be familiar. As a quick recap, BitLocker encrypts selected drives and allows Windows to read the disk after boot-time conditions such as TPM, PIN, or a recovery key are satisfied. Sector data is encrypted with the FVEK, while the VMK that protects the FVEK is accessed through protectors such as TPM, TPM+PIN, or a recovery password.

We could approach this from the perspective of the encryption algorithm, but breaking modern AES in BitLocker would overturn the assumptions behind modern symmetric cryptography. If you manage that, do not report a BitLocker bug — go write cryptographic history.

From a vulnerability-research perspective, the interesting boundary is therefore where a legitimately unlocked key is propagated and when it is taken back.

As we will see in more detail, the boot and recovery process cannot be explained solely by Boot Manager or an EFI load. It performs many actions: selecting a boot target, branching into recovery, permitting access to the OS volume, and applying security decisions and policies.

When hunting bugs in a normal OS, we commonly track privileges from the logged-in user and running processes. In WinRE and the earliest boot stages, however, an ordinary user session has not even started. Rather than asking “who executed this?”, boot-time research should focus on questions like these:

  • Under what conditions did the TPM provide the BitLocker key?
  • Which boot or recovery code was selected for execution?
  • Which settings, logs, and parameters does that code trust and process?
  • How far is access to the unlocked OS volume propagated?
  • When recovery ends or an interactive tool is started, does relocking actually occur?

The issues discussed here are close to Security Feature Bypass bugs: access is permitted legitimately, but escapes its intended scope.

How can we determine how far OS-volume access actually reaches? First, we need to distinguish BitLocker’s encryption state from its access state. Locked/Unlocked and Encrypted/Decrypted do not mean the same thing.

  • Encrypted: Disk data is stored as ciphertext. This describes the form in which data is stored on disk.
  • Locked: The disk remains encrypted, but the current environment cannot use its decryption key and therefore cannot access its files. This describes whether the current environment can use the key to read the data.

An encrypted OS volume can thus be Unlocked during a normal boot or a trusted recovery operation. Conversely, relock does not encrypt the disk again; it prevents the current environment from using the BitLocker key and blocks OS-volume access again. Therefore, seeing Protection On and Lock Status: Unlocked together is not unusual.

2. WinRE is a separate trust boundary

WinRE (Windows Recovery Environment) is a pre-OS environment that can perform Startup Repair, system reset, update removal, Command Prompt, and Defender Offline scanning. It is not always running: it boots from a separate recovery image. Crucially, it must still start when Windows has a problem or when the BitLocker OS volume cannot be read immediately, so WinRE is designed as a Recovery OS separate from the OS volume.

The Recovery OS executables, DLLs, drivers, and recovery tools are commonly contained in a compressed image named winre.wim. On a typical UEFI system, bootmgfw.efi on the EFI System Partition runs as Windows Boot Manager, reads the BCD in the same area, and decides whether to boot normal Windows or take a recovery path.

When the BCD selects a WinRE RAM-disk boot, boot.sdi and winre.wim from the recovery partition are used.

  • boot.sdi: An SDI image that builds the basic structure of a virtual NTFS disk in memory.
  • winre.wim: The compressed image expanded onto that RAM disk to build the actual Recovery OS, such as the R: drive shown in the screenshots.

In other words, bootmgfw.efi and the BCD decide the entry path — which of normal Windows or WinRE, and which image, to use. The subsequently loaded boot.sdi and winre.wim provide the actual disk structure and operating tools in the selected WinRE environment.

Input processing continues even after WinRE starts from R:. The SYSTEM hive and Boot Execute determine initial execution; winpeshl.ini, startnet.cmd, and wpeinit.exe construct the WinPE shell. Then ReAgent.xml, offline-OS information, recovery logs, and task-specific settings decide which OS is targeted and which recovery task and process run.

When analyzing WinRE, it is useful to follow each stage: which entry started the image, which volumes and drivers initialization prepared, and which settings the shell and recovery task use to launch the next process and change the FVE state.

Before the case study, let us look at two classes of logic flaws previously observed in WinRE boot and recovery flows.

3.1 Boot / Recovery Object Binding Failure

Trusted WIM and Target-Volume Binding Failures

During a WinRE boot, Boot Manager follows the RAM-disk device and path supplied by the BCD to find boot.sdi and winre.wim. A Trusted WIM Boot verifies the selected WIM’s integrity and permits BitLocker OS-volume access on the assumption that WinRE will start from that image.

After the BCD determines the recovery path, Boot Manager lays boot.sdi and winre.wim out in one RAM-disk buffer as follows:

RamDiskImageBuffer = AllocateMemory(SdiSize + WimSize);LoadFileToBuffer(SdiPath, RamDiskImageBuffer, SdiSize, NULL);LoadFileToBuffer(    WimPath,    Add2Ptr(RamDiskImageBuffer, SdiSize),    WimSize,    WimHash);WimAddress = RamDiskImageBuffer + SdiTrust->WimOffset;

In this flow, WIM A is read at RamDiskImageBuffer + SdiSize and the WimHash is computed for precisely that WIM A. The actual WinRE start address, however, is determined by SdiTrust->WimOffset. Normally, SdiTrust->WimOffset should equal SdiSize, the real start offset of WIM A.

What if that relationship is not checked? WimHash could verify WIM A while SdiTrust->WimOffset points to another WIM B in the buffer. That would make the verified recovery image differ from the recovery image that actually constructs WinRE.

There is a similar example: the target-volume-confusion vulnerability in Online PBR. It occurs after WinRE boots, when Online PBR finds its target OS. PBR uses the BCD’s osdevice to find the target volume and parses ResetSession.xml there. If it misidentifies the Recovery partition as the target OS, it can use that partition’s configuration for a PBR operation.

<WindowsRE version="2.0">  <WinreBCD id="{WinRE-BCD-GUID}" />  <WinreLocation      path="\\Recovery\\WindowsRE"      id="0"      offset="..."      guid="{RECOVERY-PARTITION-GUID}" />  <ImageLocation path="" id="0" offset="0" guid="{...}" />  <PBRImageLocation path="" id="0" offset="0" guid="{...}" index="0" /></WindowsRE>
<Operation OperationType="DecryptVolumes" TargetVolume="C:\" />

The core issue was that the configuration read from the Recovery partition was not verified as belonging to the real target OS. If its DecryptVolumes entry named a BitLocker-protected OS volume, PBR could process it as a normal recovery operation without restriction. In effect, it could remove protection from the OS volume by using PBR’s decryption authority even without the user entering a recovery key or disabling BitLocker protection.

Both patterns point to the same research question: throughout a boot transition, do the verified WIM, the selected WIM, and the OS volume being opened continue to refer to the same object?

3.2 Recovery Access Scope Bypass

Recovery Access Scope Bypass

Some boot-time operations, such as Offline Scan, need to read the OS volume. Because Offline Scan must inspect that volume, WinRE runs it with the BitLocker volume auto-unlocked.

For example, a published case described a vulnerable path in which a trusted scanning tool could launch an unintended child process through an Offline Scan setting in ReAgent.xml. The problem was not necessarily the scanner itself; it was the lack of validation that the same access level should extend to the next process created by that tool.

Normally, opening a dangerous tool such as cmd.exe should first relock the OS volume so it cannot be read without a recovery key. In the vulnerable path, however, the Offline Scanner-permitted tttracer.exe could receive cmd.exe as an argument. Since relock had not occurred, cmd.exe could inherit exposure to an OS volume that was already open.

For boot-time research, it is therefore important to trace which configuration a scheduled tool reads, whether it can create child processes, and whether relock runs before the operation ends.

The implementations of these two WinRE issue types differ, but they ask the same question:

Does the access scope selected or permitted at every stage by its trust conditions remain within its intended bounds through the next stage’s configuration parsing, process execution, and relock?

The object may be a recovery image, a target OS volume, or a process to execute. The access scope is the unlocked state of the BitLocker OS volume and the point at which it is re-locked.

Let us apply that question to the following practical flow.

4. CVE-2026-45585

Now we will trace the WinRE recovery-input and access-scope issues above as one execution chain. This case study targets the publicly disclosed FsTx recovery path in CVE-2026-45585.

4.1 Core structure and research question

Starting from the WinRE components autofstx.exe and Fstx.dll, the question is whether an FsTx artifact processed as recovery data during WinRE initialization can affect the BitLocker OS-volume access boundary. The controlled input in this study is an FsTx record on a USB volume.

USB: System Volume Information\FsTx→ WinRE BootExecute: autofstx.exe→ FsTx.dll: in-doubt transaction rollback→ delete X:\Windows\System32\winpeshl.ini→ winpeshl.exe: cmd.exe /K startnet.cmd fallback→ OS-volume access before RecEnv.exe / RelockVolumes()

As a preview: while an FsTx record is processed for rollback, a LinkPath pointing to X:\Windows\System32\winpeshl.ini causes the rollback result to prevent the current WinRE instance from finding RecEnv.exe. It launches the cmd.exe /K startnet.cmd fallback instead. Let us see why this Security Feature Bypass occurs.

4.2 Test conditions and baseline state

Windows 11 Pro 24H2 VM
TPM enabled/ready, Secure Boot enabled
WinRE enabled
BitLocker OS volume C: enabled

The reproduction environment was a Windows 11 Pro 24H2 VM with TPM and Secure Boot enabled, as well as WinRE and the BitLocker OS volume enabled. TPM and a Recovery Password were used together as key protectors.

PS C:\> manage-bde -status C:Volume C: [OS Volume]    Size:                 63.00 GB    BitLocker Version:    2.0    Conversion Status:    Fully Encrypted    Percentage Encrypted: 100.0%    Encryption Method:    XTS-AES 128    Protection Status:    Protection On    Lock Status:          Unlocked    Key Protectors:        TPM        Numerical PasswordPS C:\> manage-bde -protectors -get C:Volume C: [OS Volume]    TPM:      ID: {<TPM-PROTECTOR-GUID>}      PCR Validation Profile:        7, 11    Numerical Password:      ID: {<RECOVERY-PROTECTOR-GUID>}PS C:\> reagentc /infoWindows Recovery Environment (Windows RE)and system reset configuration    Windows RE status:    Enabled    Windows RE location:  \\?\GLOBALROOT\device\                           harddisk0\partition<RECOVERY>\Recovery\WindowsRE    BCD identifier:       {<WINRE-BCD-GUID>}

One possible source of confusion is that “Lock Status: Unlocked” while booted normally simply means that Windows is using its own volume. It does not mean BitLocker protection is disabled.

For the reproduction check, I created a marker file on the OS volume:

mkdir C:\yk_labecho YK_MARKER > C:\yk_lab\marker.txt

I also confirmed that the HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\RecoveryEnvironment\FailRelock value was absent.

According to Microsoft documentation, a TPM-only environment satisfying the PCR[7] supported-device condition can auto-unlock a BitLocker OS volume when started from trusted WinRE. Which execution paths can access that auto-unlocked volume before RecEnv.exe relocks it?

4.3 Normal flow and the relock path bypassed by FsTx

Once trusted WinRE begins initialization, the normal flow has winpeshl.exe read winpeshl.ini and launch RecEnv.exe. RecEnv.exe calls RelockVolume() before displaying the recovery UI.

CImmersiveRecoveryUi::Run  └─ CRecoveryEnvironment::RelockVolumes      └─ CFveUtil::RelockAllVolumes          └─ CFveUtil::RelockVolume

CImmersiveRecoveryUi::Run is both the recovery-UI entry point and the relock trigger. Before drawing its UI, it calls CRecoveryEnvironment::RelockVolumes; if that fails, it logs “Failed to relock volumes. 0x%08x Shutting down.” and exits.

// CImmersiveRecoveryUi::Run, summarizedif (!relockHandled) {    HRESULT hr = CRecoveryEnvironment::RelockVolumes(*this);    if (FAILED(hr)) {        WdsSetupLogMessageW(..., "Failed to relock volumes. 0x%08x  Shutting down.", hr);        goto shutdown;    }    CRecoveryEnvironment::UnlockVolumes(*this, 0);    relockHandled = 1;}

The internal RelockVolumes dispatcher, CFveUtil::RelockAllVolumes, iterates volumes with FindFirstVolumeW/FindNextVolumeW and calls CFveUtil::RelockVolume for each volume.

// CFveUtil::RelockAllVolumes, summarizedwhile (FindNextVolume(...)) {    if (Utils::GetDriveLetterForVolumeMountPoint(szVolumeName, letter, MAX_PATH))        continue;    if (!CFveUtil::RelockVolume(this, letter))        break;}return 31; // relock failed

The normal path is:

winpeshl.exe → winpeshl.ini → RecEnv.exe → RelockVolumes() → recovery UI

This case study does not tamper with or make RelockVolume() fail. Instead, if winpeshl.ini disappears and winpeshl.exe selects a fallback shell rather than RecEnv.exe, the relock path is never reached.

4.4 FsTx artifacts and the root cause

FsTx is related to TxF (Transactional NTFS), an NTFS feature that groups file operations into one transaction. For example, creating a file, renaming it, and adding a hard link elsewhere can be started as a group. Once all work is finished, the transaction is committed and the changes remain. If power is lost or an error occurs midway, uncommitted work is rolled back to its prior state.

FsTx metadata is the record needed for that rollback. It logs file operations that began and paths that were to be created or removed under System Volume Information\FsTx on a volume. WinRE’s autofstx.exe and FsTx.dll read those records and process the recorded operations to restore the file system to its pre-transaction state.

For this test, I placed only an FsTx artifact on USB — not an executable.

FsTx\└─ 95F62703B343F111A92A005056975458\   ├─ FsTxLogs\   │  ├─ FsTxKtmLog.blf   │  ├─ FsTxKtmLogContainer00000000000000000001   │  ├─ FsTxKtmLogContainer00000000000000000002   │  ├─ FsTxLog.blf   │  ├─ FsTxLogContainer00000000000000000001   │  └─ FsTxLogContainer00000000000000000002   └─ FsTxTemp\       └─ 98F62703B343F111A92A005056975458

The root cause has two connected steps: autofstx.exe accepts an external volume as an FsTx recovery candidate, then FsTx.dll processes an absolute path in a rollback record.

The reason to place only an FsTx artifact on the USB was to determine whether WinRE finds it as a normal recovery log and rolls back the file operation left in the transaction record. If that record’s LinkPath points to X:\Windows\System32\winpeshl.ini, the rollback deletes that file.

TargetPath (source data) = \??\C:\Windows\win.iniLinkPath (new link)      = \??\X:\Windows\System32\winpeshl.ini

This represents creating a hard link named winpeshl.ini from win.ini. Critically, to trigger the issue, the creation operation must be left uncommitted, with only the log remaining.

When WinRE finds a stored but unfinished transaction, it rolls it back for file-system consistency. Reverting hard-link creation means deleting the new link:

File = DoCreateFile(..., LinkPath /* = X:\...\winpeshl.ini */, ...);dispositionFlags = 0x11;   // DELETE | POSIXSetFileInformationByHandle(File);   // → deletes LinkPath directly

The rollback code therefore means “delete the file at LinkPath.” There is no apparent verification that the link was truly created by this transaction. winpeshl.ini originally comes from winre.wim and is unrelated to the transaction, yet the rollback treats the file at LinkPath as its deletion target.

How autofstx.exe replays FsTx transactions

For autofstx.exe 26100.1, the OS version used in this reproduction, the PDB reveals this flow:

main  → AutoFsTxSession::Init      → LdrLoadDll("FsTx.dll")  → AutoFsTxSession::RunSession      → VolumeContext::FindFsTxVolumes      → FsTxSessionSet::ScanSessions      → FsTxCreateRecoverySession      → FsTxEnumTransactions      → FsTxPerformRecovery

autofstx.exe does not roll back FsTx logs itself. It first finds volumes containing System Volume Information\FsTx and passes them as recovery targets; the dynamically loaded FsTx.dll performs the log parsing and rollback.

The relevant points are therefore autofstx.exe’s volume selection and FsTx.dll’s LinkPath handling. The former passes the USB FsTx artifact to WinRE recovery code, while the latter deletes X:\Windows\System32\winpeshl.ini specified in the record.

VolumeContext::FindFsTxVolumes enumerates the volume-GUID namespace with FindFirstVolumeW/FindNextVolumeW, finds a mount path that is a drive-letter root (A:\${b} throughZ:${b}), and adds a volume to the recovery candidates if it contains a System Volume Information\FsTx directory.

// VolumeContext::FindFsTxVolumes, summarizedGetVolumePathNamesForVolumeNameW(volumeGuid, mountPaths, ...);for (WCHAR *i = mountPaths; *i; i += wcslen(i) + 1) {    if (wcslen(i) == 3 && i[1] == L':' && i[2] == L'\\') {        driveLetter = *i;        break;    }}if (!driveLetter) continue;wcscat_s(path, MAX_PATH, L"System Volume Information\\FsTx");DWORD attrs = GetFileAttributesW(path);if (attrs == INVALID_FILE_ATTRIBUTES || !(attrs & FILE_ATTRIBUTE_DIRECTORY))    continue;candidates.push_back(volume);

Thus, the function selects recovery targets based on the presence of a drive letter and a System Volume Information\FsTx directory. An external USB with that structure is accepted as a recovery candidate, then AutoFsTxSession::RunSession finds its session and starts replay with FsTxPerformRecovery(handle, 0, 60000).

// Recovery handling for each candidate inside AutoFsTxSession::RunSessionmessageContext = (AutoFsTxSession *)((char *)session + 96);if (recoveryStatus >= 0) {    FsTxMessageContext::OutputMessage(messageContext, 2u, 0x3F4u, sessionIndex);    v50 = 1;} else {    FsTxMessageContext::OutputMessage(messageContext, 8u, 0x3F5u, sessionIndex, recoveryStatus);    v50 = 0;}*(_BYTE *)(fsTxSession + 98) = v50;FsTxSession::CloseSession((FsTxSession *)fsTxSession, closeReason);// Actual replay call (export of dynamically loaded FsTx.dll)pfnFsTxPerformRecovery = (int64 (*)(int64, QWORD, int64))g_FsTxPerformRecovery;FsTxVolumes = pfnFsTxPerformRecovery(sessionHandle, 0, 60000);

autofstx.exe does not process the work performed by FsTx.dll directly; it only receives the success or failure result and logs it. Deletion of winpeshl.ini happens in FsTx.dll’s replay stage.

Now let us look at the code where the USB volume becomes a recovery candidate and where rollback processes LinkPath.

Root-cause code

1. VolumeContext::FindFsTxVolumes — accepting an untrusted USB as a recovery candidate

BaseAddress = FindFirstVolumeW(Str);// ← Enumerates every volume; no fixed/removable/USB distinction// Is there a drive-letter root such as X:\?if ( v20 == 3 && i[1] == 58 /* ':' */ && i[2] == 92 /* '\' */ && (letter a-z/A-Z) )    v17 = *i;                              // Obtain the drive letter// Sole eligibility check: does "<drive>:\System Volume Information\FsTx" exist?wcscat_s(Str, 0x104u, L"System Volume Information\\FsTx");FileAttributesW = GetFileAttributesW(Str);if ( FileAttributesW == -1 || (FileAttributesW & 0x10) == 0 )    v7 = 0;                                // Reject if the directory is absentLABEL_54:    v23 = AutoChkMalloc(0x48u);            // ★ This is where the volume becomes a recovery candidate    ...    v24[66] = v7;                          // v7(+0x42): whether recovery runs; RunSession uses it

As introduced earlier, a volume with a drive letter and a System Volume Information\FsTx directory is handled as a recovery candidate.

2. PerformOperationRollbackRecovery (op == 5) — cross-volume deletion of winpeshl.ini

if ( opType == 5 )   // Roll back HARDLINK creation.{    TempRootPath = (wchar_t *)GetTempRootPath(recoveryCtx, linkPath, linkPath);    v30 = TempRootPath;    if ( TempRootPath )    {        v43 = AddPathToPathSet((PRTL_DYNAMIC_HASH_TABLE)(recoveryCtx + 2152), TempRootPath);        RtlNtStatusToDosError(v43);    }    HIDWORD(v115) = 0;    File = (HANDLE)DoCreateFile(recoveryCtx, 0, (_DWORD)Name, (unsigned int)&v135, *(_DWORD *)(opRecord + 12) & 8);    // ↑ Opens Name, record path[1] = \??\X:\Windows\System32\winpeshl.ini,    //   directly as an absolute NT path. There is no check that its volume    //   matches the source volume of this transaction.    if ( File != (HANDLE)-1LL || (LastWin32Error = RtlGetLastWin32Error()) != 0 )    {        v44 = LastWin32Error;        if ( LastWin32Error == 2 ) // No link: skip        {            LastWin32Error = 0;            goto LABEL_225;        }        if ( !LastWin32Error )        {            dispositionFlags = 17;            // 0x11 = DELETE | POSIX — unvalidated cross-volume deletion            SetFileInformationByHandle(File);            goto LABEL_225;        }    }}

The problem is that DoCreateFile() opens the record’s Name directly as an absolute NT path and does not confirm that the file was the link created by this transaction. If a USB transaction record sets LinkPath to X:\Windows\System32\winpeshl.ini, FsTx.dll treats the existing file — unrelated to the USB source volume — as a link that must be reverted. With dispositionFlags = 0x11, that path is removed with a POSIX delete.

4.5 Reproduction result

First, I placed the FsTx artifact on USB drive E:. A normal boot into WinRE would display the recovery UI. Let us look at the result after inserting the USB and booting into WinRE.

After connecting the USB containing the intended FsTx artifact and booting into WinRE, X:\Windows\System32\cmd.exe appears instead of the normal recovery UI. Files such as winpeshl.exe and winpeshl.log remain, but winpeshl.ini — which should be in the same directory — cannot be found. This indicates it was deleted by rollback.

winpeshl.log also records execution of X:\Windows\System32\cmd.exe /K startnet.cmd, confirming that the cmd.exe fallback ran.

winre_access_proof.txt contains WinRE_ACCESS_PROOF and a timestamp, and the marker file created from the WinRE session shows that writing to the file succeeded.

Closing thoughts

In this article, we directly followed the WinRE boot process and recovery code, which are easy to overlook. The next time you accidentally enter Windows recovery mode, perhaps you will remember that behind the blue recovery screen, a separate WinRE environment has booted and is preparing and running recovery functions.

Did you enjoy the WinRE series? In the next article, we will go one step earlier than WinRE and return to Boot Manager to look at BitPixie: why an older signed Boot Manager can be run again, and what happens during the PXE transition that follows. Please look forward to it!

References

  1. Alon Leviev, Netanel Ben Simon, “BitUnlocker: Leveraging Windows Recovery to Extract BitLocker Secrets,” Microsoft Security Blog, August 13, 2025.
    https://techcommunity.microsoft.com/blog/microsoft-security-blog/bitunlocker-leveraging-windows-recovery-to-extract-bitlocker-secrets/4442806

  2. Nightmare-Eclipse, “YellowKey: BitLocker Bypass Vulnerability,” GitHub, 2026. (Archived copy)
    https://github.com/meltingscales/YellowKey

  3. Microsoft Security Response Center, “CVE-2026-45585: Windows BitLocker Security Feature Bypass Vulnerability,” Microsoft Security Update Guide, 2026.
    https://msrc.microsoft.com/update-guide/vulnerability/CVE-2026-45585

  4. Microsoft, “WinPE: Create Apps,” Microsoft Learn.
    https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-hardware/manufacture/desktop/winpe-create-apps

item.title: [Research] Unlocking BitLocker: 암호화 안깨고 취약점 찾는 방법 - Part 2 (KR)
item.content:encoded:
Part 1: https://hackyboiz.github.io/2026/01/22/banda/BitLocker_part1/ko/

0. Overview

안녕하세요! 동상이몽 팀으로 찾아온 banda입니다. 조금 오래 전이긴 한데, 제가 작성했던 BitLocker 연구글을 기억하시나요? 저는 그동안 도를 닦느라 잠시 잊고있었던 BitLocker를 다시 한번 파보기로 했습니다

지난 Part 1에서는 BitLocker가 사용하는 XTS-AES의 특징과, 암호문 무결성 부재를 이용해 시스템 동작을 실패시키는 매커니즘을 활용한 CrashXTS를 살펴봤어요. CrashXTS에서 공격자는 암호화된 디스크에 원하는 평문을 써넣을 수는 없었어요. 대신 특정 암호문 블록을 변조해 대응하는 평문 블록을 예측 불가능하게 손상시킬 수 있었습니다.

다만 앞선 사례처럼 AES 암호화된 데이터를 직접 해독하는건 매우 어렵기 때문에, 앞으로는 암호 알고리즘보다 키가 해제되고 사용되는 과정에 집중해봅시다! 긴 시간 끝에 돌아온 이번 글에서는 WinRE와 Boot Manager의 신뢰 관계에서 발생하는 흥미로운 취약점들을 살펴보겠습니다.

1. WinRE는 왜 BitLocker의 공격 표면이 되었을까

이전에 BitLocker을 사용해본 적이 있다면 아마 익숙한 창일 것 같은데요. 지난 파트 내용을 복습해보면 BitLocker는 특정 선택한 드라이브를 암호화하는 기능이고, 부팅할 때 TPM/PIN/복구 키 같은 조건을 확인해 통과하면 Windows가 디스크를 읽게 해주는 기능입니다. 이때 섹터 데이터는 FVEK로 암호화되고, FVEK를 보호하는 VMK를 얻는 경로는 TPM, TPM+PIN, 복구 암호 등의 보호기로 정해집니다.

물론 암호화 알고리즘의 관점으로 접근해볼 수도 있겠지만, BitLocker에서 현대 AES 자체를 깨는건 현대 대칭키 암호의 전제를 흔드는 것일 수 있습니다.🤯 (성공하시면 비트로커 취약점 제보를 하시면 안되고 암호학 역사를 쓰러 가셔야 합니다..)

따라서 저희가 이번에 취약점 분석 관점으로 볼 것은 정상적으로 풀린 키가 어디까지 전달되고 언제 회수되는지 경계를 확인하는 것입니다.

이후 자세히 설명하겠지만, 부팅과 복구 과정은 단순히 부팅매니저나 EFI 로드만으로는 설명되지 않는게 많습니다. 그 점에서 더 흥미로운 표면이라고 볼 수 있는데요. 부팅 과정에서도 부팅 대상을 선택하거나, 복구 작업에 분기하거나, OS volume 접근 허용하거나, 보안 결정이나 정책을 설정하는 등 다양한 작업이 수행됩니다.

흥미로운 점은 보통 일반 OS에서 버그헌팅을 할 때는 로그인한 사용자와 실행 중인 프로세스를 기준으로 권한을 추적하는데, WinRE나 부팅 초기 단계에서는 일반 사용자 로그인 세션이 아직 시작도 되지 않은 상태라는 것이죠.😱 그러면 권한 경계를 안보면 도대체 뭘 봐야 할까 좀 난처하기도 한데요. 부팅 과정에서는 이제 ‘누가 실행했는가?’라는 질문을 던지기보다는 아래와 같은 조건을 중점으로 확인해봐야 합니다.

  • TPM이 어떤 조건에서 BitLocker 키를 제공했는가
  • 어떤 부팅/복구 코드가 실행 대상으로 선택됐는가
  • 그 코드가 어떤 설정/로그/매개변수를 신뢰하고 처리하는가
  • OS volume이 열린 상태가 어느 프로세스까지 전달되는가
  • 복구 작업이 끝나거나 대화형 도구로 넘어갈 때 relock이 실제로 수행되는가

이번에 알아볼 문제들은 이렇게 정상적으로 허용된 접근이 의도한 범위를 벗어나는 Security Feature Bypass 유형에 가깝습니다.

그렇다면 실제로 OS volume 접근이 어디까지 이어졌는지를 어떻게 판단할 수 있을까요? 먼저 BitLocker에서 말하는 암호화 상태와 접근 상태를 나눠서 봐야 합니다. 혹시 BitLocker에서 Locked/Unlocked 상태와 Encrypted/Decrypted 상태가 서로 다르다는 것을 아시나요?

  • Encrypted: 디스크의 데이터가 암호문으로 저장되어 있는 상태. 즉, 디스크에 데이터가 어떤 형태로 저장되어 있는가에 대한 상태.
  • Locked: 디스크는 그대로 암호화되어 있지만, 현재 환경에서는 복호화 키를 사용할 수 없어 파일에 접근할 수 없는 상태. 즉, 현재 환경에서 그 데이터를 읽을 키를 사용할 수 있는가에 대한 상태.

즉, 암호화된 OS volume에서도 정상 부팅이나 신뢰된 복구 작업 중에는 Unlocked 상태가 될 수 있습니다. 반대로 relock은 디스크를 다시 암호화하는 과정이 아니라, 현재 환경에서 BitLocker 키를 사용할 수 없게 만들어 OS volume 접근을 다시 막는 동작입니다. 그래서 Protection On과 Lock Status: Unlocked가 함께 표시되어도 딱히 이상하지 않다고 할 수 있겠죠.

2. WinRE는 별도의 신뢰 경계

WinRE(Windows Recovery Environment)는 시작 복구, 시스템 초기화, 업데이트 제거, 명령 프롬프트, Defender 오프라인 검사 등을 수행할 수 있도록 동작하는 부팅 과정에서의 Pre-OS라고 볼 수 있습니다. WinRE는 평소에 계속 열리는건 아니고, 별도의 복구 이미지로 부팅합니다. 중요한 것은 Windows에 문제가 생겼거나 BitLocker OS volume을 바로 읽지 못하는 상황에서 이 복구 도구는 정상적으로 시작되어야 하므로, WinRE는 OS volume과 분리된 Recovery OS로 구성된다는 점입니다.

이 Recovery OS의 실행 파일/DLL/드라이버와 복구 도구는 보통 winre.wim이라는 압축 이미지에 들어가 있습니다. winre.wim은 WinPE 기반의 Recovery OS의 실행 파일, DLL, 드라이버, 복구 도구가 압축된 WIM 이미지입니다. 일반적인 UEFI 시스템에서는 EFI System Partition의 bootmgfw.efi가 Windows Boot Manager로 실행되고, 같은 영역의 BCD를 읽어 일반 Winows 대신 어떤 복구 경로로 부팅을 할지를 결정합니다.

이후 BCD가 WinRE RAM disk 부팅을 선택하면, 복구 파티션에 있는 boot.sdi와 winre.wim이 사용됩니다.

  • boot.sdi: RAM에 가상 NTFS 디스크의 기본 구조를 만들기 위한 SDI 이미지
  • winre.wim: 그 RAM 디스크 위에 풀려 R: 드라이브 환경(스크린샷의 경우)에서 실제 Recovery OS를 구성하는 압축 이미지

즉, bootmgfw.efi와 BCD가 일반 Windows와 WinRE 중 어느 경로와 이미지를 사용할지 진입 경로를 결정하는 역할을 한다면, 이후 로드되는 boot.sdi와 winre.wim은 선택된 WinRE 환경에서 실질적인 디스크 구조와 운영 도구를 제공하는 역할을 담당합니다.

WinRE가 R:에서 시작된 뒤에도 입력 처리는 계속됩니다. SYSTEM hive와 Boot Execute가 초기 실행을 정하고, winpeshl.ini, startnet.cmd, wpeinit.exe가 WinPE shell을 구성합니다. 그리고 이후 ReAgent.xml, offline OS 정보, 복구 로그, 작업별 설정이 어떤 OS를 대상으로 어떤 recovery task와 process를 실행할지 결정합니다.

즉 WinRE 연구에서 표면을 분석해본다면, 어떤 entry가 이 image를 시작했는지, 초기화 코드가 어떤 volume과 driver를 준비했는지, shell과 recovery task가 어떤 설정을 바탕으로 다음 process와 FVE 상태를 바꾸는지 단계별로 따라가보는 것이 좋겠죠?

이러한 시야를 바탕으로, Case Study에 들어가기 전 기존에 WinRE boot, recovery flow에서 실제로 나타났던 로직 버그를 두 가지 유형으로 살펴보겠습니다.

3.1 Boot / Recovery Object Binding Failure

Trusted WIM and Target-Volume Binding Failures

WinRE로 부팅 과정에서 기본적으로 Boot Manager는 BCD가 준 ramdisk device와 path를 따라 boot.sdi와 winre.wim을 찾는다고 했죠. Trusted WIM Boot는 선택된 WIM의 무결성을 확인하고, 이어 WinRE가 그 이미지에서 시작될 것을 전제로 BitLocker OS volume 접근을 허용합니다.

BCD가 복구 경로를 결정한 뒤에는 Boot Manager가 다음과 같이 boot.sdi와 winre.wim을 하나의 RAM-disk buffer에 배치합니다.

RamDiskImageBuffer = AllocateMemory(SdiSize + WimSize);LoadFileToBuffer(SdiPath, RamDiskImageBuffer, SdiSize, NULL);LoadFileToBuffer(    WimPath,    Add2Ptr(RamDiskImageBuffer, SdiSize),    WimSize,    WimHash);WimAddress = RamDiskImageBuffer + SdiTrust->WimOffset;

이 흐름에서 WIM A는 RamDiskImageBuffer + SdiSize에 읽히고, WimHash는 바로 그 WIM A에 대해 계산됩니다. 반면 실제 WinRE 시작 주소는 SdiTrust→WimOffset으로 결정되는데요. 정상적인 경우에는 SdiTrust→WimOffset이 WIM A의 실제 시작 offset인 SdiSize와 같았어야 합니다.

그런데 이 경로에 대한 검증 체크가 없다면 어떻게 될까요? WimHash는 WIM A를 검증했는데, SdiTrust→WimOffset은 buffer 안의 다른 WIM B를 가리킬 수 있게 되는 취약점이 발생할 수 있습니다. 즉, 검증한 recovery 이미지와 실제로 WinRE를 구성한 복구 이미지가 불일치할 수 있게 되는 취약점이 발생할 수 있었습니다.

비슷한 다른 사례를 확인해볼까요? Online PBR의 target-volume confusion 취약점이 있습니다. WinRE가 부팅된 뒤의 시점을 다루는데요. WinRE가 부팅된 후 Online PBR이 target OS를 찾는 단계에서 발생하는 취약점입니다. PBR은 BCD의 osdevice로 target volume을 찾고 그곳의 ResetSession.xml이라는 설정 파일을 읽으면서 파싱하는데, Recovery partition을 target OS로 잘못 식별하면 Recovery partition의 설정을 PBR 작업에 사용할 수 있었습니다.

<WindowsRE version="2.0">  <WinreBCD id="{WinRE-BCD-GUID}" />  <WinreLocation      path="\\Recovery\\WindowsRE"      id="0"      offset="..."      guid="{RECOVERY-PARTITION-GUID}" />  <ImageLocation path="" id="0" offset="0" guid="{...}" />  <PBRImageLocation path="" id="0" offset="0" guid="{...}" index="0" /></WindowsRE>
<Operation OperationType="DecryptVolumes" TargetVolume="C:\" />

핵심 문제는 Recovery partition에서 읽은 설정이 실제 target OS의 설정인지 검증을 안했다는 것인데요. 설정의 DecryptVolumes가 BitLocker로 보호된 OS volume을 지정하면, PBR은 이걸 아무런 제약 없이 정상적인 복구 작업으로 처리해버릴 수 있었습니다. 이게 왜 문제가 되냐면 사용자가 recovery key를 입력하거나 BitLocker 보호를 해제하지도 않았는데도 PBR의 복호화 권한을 이용해 OS volume 보호를 제거해버릴 수도 있다는 것이죠.😱 강력한 취약점이었습니다.

즉, 두 패턴이 시사하는 바는 검증한 wim/선택한 wim/열려는 OS volume이 부팅 전환 내내 같은 대상을 가리키는지, 일관성을 유지하는지를 유의깊게 보라는 의미겠죠?

3.2 Recovery Access Scope Bypass

Recovery Access Scope Bypass

부팅 과정에서는 Offline Scan처럼 OS volume을 읽어야 하는 작업도 존재합니다. Offline Scan은 기본적으로 OS volume을 검사해야 하기 때문에 WinRE가 BitLocker volume을 auto-unlock한 상태에서 실행됩니다.

예를들어 공개된 사례에서는 ReAgent.xml의 Offline Scan 설정을 통해 신뢰된 검사 도구가 의도하지 않은 child process를 실행할 수 있었던 취약한 경로가 다뤄진 적이 있습니다. 중요한 부분은 검사 도구 자체가 신뢰된 프로그램이더가도, 그 도구가 만드는 다음 프로세스까지 같은 수준으로 허용해도 되는지를 딱히 검증을 하지 않은게 문제가 되었죠.

보통 cmd.exe같은 위험한 도구를 열면 먼저 relock을 해서 recovery key 없이는 OS volume이 못 읽어야 하는데, 위 취약점을 이용하면 Offline Scaner가 허용한 tttracer.exe가 인자로 cmd.exe를 받아올 수 있었고, relock이 열려있었기 때문에 cmd.exe가 이미 열려 있던 OS volume이 그대로 노출될 수가 있었습니다.

따라서 부팅 과정에서 예약된 도구가 어떤 configuration을 읽는지, child process를 만들 수 있는지, 작업이 끝나기 전에 relock이 실행되는지를 모두 따라가보는 것도 연구 관점에서 중요하겠죠?

정리하면, 두 WinRE 유형의 구현은 다르지만, 공통 질문은 같았습니다.

각 단계가 신뢰 조건에 따라 선택하거나 허용한 접근 범위가, 다음 단계 설정 해석, process 실행, relock까지 의도한 범위 내로 유지되는가?

여기서 대상은 recovery image, target OS volume, 실행할 process가 될 수 있고, 접근 범위는 BitLocker OS volume의 unlock 상태와 re-lock 시점이 됩니다.

그러면 이제 이 질문을 제가 실습한 두 흐름에 대입해보겠습니다.

4. CVE-2026-45585

이제 앞에서 정리한 WinRE recovery input과 access scope 문제를 하나의 실행 chain으로 따라가볼 차례가 되었습니다.. 이 Case Study는 공개된 CVE-2026-45585의 FsTx recovery 경로를 대상으로 합니다.

4.1 핵심 구조와 연구 질문

이 흐름 출발점은 WinRE 구성요소인 autofstx.exe나 Fstx.dll을 기점으로, 부팅 중 WinRE 초기화를 하는 시점에서 FsTx artifact가 복구 data로 처리될 때, 그 결과가 BitLocker OS volume 접근 경계까지 이어질 수 있는지 확장해보는 것입니다. 우리가 이번에 제어할 입력값은 USB volume의 FsTx record입니다.

USB: System Volume Information\FsTx→ WinRE BootExecute: autofstx.exe→ FsTx.dll: in-doubt transaction rollback→ X:\Windows\System32\winpeshl.ini 삭제→ winpeshl.exe: cmd.exe /K startnet.cmd fallback→ RecEnv.exe / RelockVolumes() 이전의 OS volume 접근

살짝 스포를 해보자면 FsTx record를 rollback 작업으로 처리하는 과정에서 record 안의 LinkPath가 X:\Windows\System32\winpeshl.ini에 가리켜지면, rollback 결과가 현재 실행 중인 WinRE의 RecEnv.exe를 찾지 못하고, 대신 cmd.exe /K startnet.cmd fallback을 실행하게 되는데요. 왜 이런 Security Feature Bypass가 발생하게 되었는지 한번 확인해봅시다!

4.2 실험 조건과 기준 상태

Windows 11 Pro 24H2 VM
TPM enabled/ready, Secure Boot enabled
WinRE enabled
BitLocker OS 볼륨 C: 활성 상태

재현 환경은 TPM과 Secure Boot가 켜진 Windows 11 Pro 24H2 VM이며, WinRE와 BitLocker OS volume을 활성화한 상태였습니다. 키 보호기는 TPM과 Recovery Password를 함께 사용했습니다.

PS C:\> manage-bde -status C:Volume C: [OS Volume]    Size:                 63.00 GB    BitLocker Version:    2.0    Conversion Status:    Fully Encrypted    Percentage Encrypted: 100.0%    Encryption Method:    XTS-AES 128    Protection Status:    Protection On    Lock Status:          Unlocked    Key Protectors:        TPM        Numerical PasswordPS C:\> manage-bde -protectors -get C:Volume C: [OS Volume]    TPM:      ID: {<TPM-PROTECTOR-GUID>}      PCR Validation Profile:        7, 11            Numerical Password:      ID: {<RECOVERY-PROTECTOR-GUID>}PS C:\> reagentc /infoWindows Recovery Environment (Windows RE)and system reset configuration    Windows RE status:    Enabled    Windows RE location:  \\?\GLOBALROOT\device\                           harddisk0\partition<RECOVERY>\Recovery\WindowsRE    BCD identifier:       {<WINRE-BCD-GUID>}

이런 식으로 상태를 세팅해주면 되는데요. 여기서 헷갈리실 수 있는 부분은 정상 Windows로 부팅된 상태에서 잠금 상태: 잠금 해제됨은 OS가 자기 볼륨을 사용 중이라는 뜻이지, BitLocker 보호가 꺼졌다는 뜻은 아닙니다.

재현 확인용으로는 OS 볼륨에 marker 파일을 만들어 두었습니다.

mkdir C:\yk_labecho YK_MARKER > C:\yk_lab\marker.txt

또한 HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\RecoveryEnvironment\FailRelock 값이 없는 상태를 확인했습니다.

Microsoft 문서 기준으로 PCR[7] 지원 장치 조건을 만족하는 TPM-only 환경에서는, 신뢰된 WinRE로 시작될 때 BitLocker OS volume이 auto-unlock될 수 있었습니다. 그렇다면 auto-unlock된 OS volume은 RecEnv.exe의 relock 전까지 어떤 실행 경로에 노출되었을까요?

4.3 정상 흐름과 relock 경로 (이 FsTx 흐름이 우회하는 지점)

기본적으로 신뢰된 WinRE가 초기화가 시작되면, 정상 흐름에서는 winpeshl.exe가 winpeshl.ini를 읽고 RecEnv.exe를 실행합니다. RecEnv.exe는 복구 UI를 띄우기 전에 RelockVolume()를 호출합니다.

CImmersiveRecoveryUi::Run  └─ CRecoveryEnvironment::RelockVolumes      └─ CFveUtil::RelockAllVolumes          └─ CFveUtil::RelockVolume

CImmersiveRecoveryUi::Run은 복구 UI 엔트리이자 relock 트리거입니다. UI를 그리기 전에 CRecoveryEnvironment::RelockVolumes를 호출하고, 실패하면 "Failed to relock volumes. 0x%08x Shutting down." 로그를 남기고 종료합니다.

// CImmersiveRecoveryUi::Run 요약if (!relockHandled) {    HRESULT hr = CRecoveryEnvironment::RelockVolumes(*this);    if (FAILED(hr)) {        WdsSetupLogMessageW(..., "Failed to relock volumes. 0x%08x  Shutting down.", hr);        goto shutdown;    }    CRecoveryEnvironment::UnlockVolumes(*this, 0);    relockHandled = 1;}

RelockVolumes 내부 dispatcher인 CFveUtil::RelockAllVolumes는 FindFirstVolumeW/FindNextVolumeW로 volume을 순회하고, 각 volume에 CFveUtil::RelockVolume을 호출합니다.

// CFveUtil::RelockAllVolumes 요약while (FindNextVolume(...)) {    if (Utils::GetDriveLetterForVolumeMountPoint(szVolumeName, letter, MAX_PATH))        continue;    if (!CFveUtil::RelockVolume(this, letter))        break;}return 31; // relock failed

정상 경로는 아래와 같습니다.

winpeshl.exe → winpeshl.ini → RecEnv.exe → RelockVolumes() → recovery UI

이 Case Study에서는 RelockVolume() 자체를 변조하거나 실패시키지 않습니다. 다만 winpeshl.ini가 없어졌을 때 winpeshl.exe가 RecEnv.exe 대신 fallback shell을 선택한다면, 결국 위 relock path에는 도달하지 못합니다.

4.4 FsTx artifact와 root cause

앞에서 계속 언급되었던 FsTx가 뭔지 많이 궁금하셨을 텐데요. FsTx는 TxF(Transactional NTFS)는 여러 파일 작업을 하나의 transaction으로 묶어 처리하는 NTFS 기능입니다. 예를들어 파일을 만들고, 이름을 바꾸고, 다른 위치에 하드링크를 추가하는 작업을 묶음으로 시작할 수 있습니다. 묶음 작업이 모두 끝나면 commit되어 변경 사항이 남고, 중간에 전원이 꺼지거나 오류가 나면 commit되지 않은 작업이 rollback되어 이전 상태로 돌아가는 특징을 가지고 있습니다.

이때 FsTx metadata는 바로 이 rollback에 필요한 기록입니다. 어떤 파일 작업이 시작되었는지, 어떤 경로를 만들거나 지우려고 했는지 같은 정보가 volume의 System Volume Information\FsTx 아래 로그에 남습니다. 그리고 WinRE의 autofstx.exe와 FsTx.dll이 이 기록을 읽고, 파일 시스템을 transaction 이전 상태로 되돌리기 위해 기록된 작업을 처리하기 시작합니다.

이번 실습에서는 USB에 executable을 두지 않고 FsTx artifact만 배치했습니다.

FsTx\└─ 95F62703B343F111A92A005056975458\   ├─ FsTxLogs\   │  ├─ FsTxKtmLog.blf   │  ├─ FsTxKtmLogContainer00000000000000000001   │  ├─ FsTxKtmLogContainer00000000000000000002   │  ├─ FsTxLog.blf   │  ├─ FsTxLogContainer00000000000000000001   │  └─ FsTxLogContainer00000000000000000002   └─ FsTxTemp\      └─ 98F62703B343F111A92A005056975458

root cause는 두 단계가 이어지는 데 있습니다. autofstx.exe가 외부 volume을 FsTx recovery candidate로 넣고, FsTx.dll이 rollback record의 absolute path를 처리합니다.

이 실습에서 USB에 FsTx artifact만 배치한 이유는, WinRE가 이를 정상 복구 log로 찾아 transaction record에 남은 파일 작업을 rollback하는지를 보기 위해서입니다. 이때 record가 가리키는 LinkPath가 X:\Windows\System32\winpeshl.ini이면, rollback 결과는 해당 파일의 삭제로 이어집니다.

TargetPath(원본 데이터) = \??\C:\Windows\win.iniLinkPath(새로 만들 링크) = \??\X:\Windows\System32\winpeshl.ini

win.ini를 원본으로 삼아 winpeshl.ini라는 새 hardlink를 만드는 작업입니다. 가장 중요한 특이점은 취약점 트리거를 위해 이 생성 작업을 commit 하지 않은 채로 로그만 남겨놓아야 한다는 것입니다.

FsTx 루틴을 생각해보면, 완료되지 않은 상태로 저장된 transaction을 WinRE가 발견하면, commit되지 않았으므로 파일시스템 일관성을 위해 rollback할 것입니다. hardlink 생성을 되돌리기 위해 새 link를 삭제하는 흐름이죠.

File = DoCreateFile(..., LinkPath /* = X:\...\winpeshl.ini */, ...);dispositionFlags = 0x11;   // DELETE | POSIXSetFileInformationByHandle(File);   // → LinkPath를 그냥 지운다

실제 rollback 코드는 다음과 같았습니다. 내용은 LinkPath 자리에 있는 파일을 삭제하라는 뜻입니다.

여기서 확인할 부분은 이 link가 실제로 해당 transaction이 만든 것인지 검증하는 과정이 보이지 않는다는 점입니다. 그래서 그냥 통과할 수 있었던 것이죠. winpeshl.ini는 원래 winre.wim에 들어 있던 파일로 transaction과 무관하지만, rollback 로직은 LinkPath에 있는 파일을 삭제 대상으로 처리합니다.

autofstx.exe가 FsTx 트랜잭션을 재생하는 과정

autofstx.exe 26100.1(제가 재현했던 OS 버전)을 PDB와 함께 보면 흐름은 다음과 같습니다.

main  → AutoFsTxSession::Init      → LdrLoadDll("FsTx.dll")  → AutoFsTxSession::RunSession      → VolumeContext::FindFsTxVolumes      → FsTxSessionSet::ScanSessions      → FsTxCreateRecoverySession      → FsTxEnumTransactions      → FsTxPerformRecovery

autofstx.exe는 FsTx log를 직접 rollback하지 않습니다. 먼저 어느 volume에 System Volume Information\FsTx가 있는지 찾아 recovery 대상으로 넘기고, 실제 log 해석과 rollback은 동적으로 로드한 FsTx.dll에 맡깁니다.

따라서 이 흐름에서는 autofstx.exe의 volume 선택과 FsTx.dll의 LinkPath 처리, 두 지점을 함께 볼겁니다. 전자가 USB FsTx artifact를 WinRE recovery code에 전달하고, 후자가 record에 적힌 X:\Windows\System32\winpeshl.ini를 삭제하기 때문이죠.

VolumeContext::FindFsTxVolumes는 FindFirstVolumeW/FindNextVolumeW로 volume GUID namespace를 열거하고, mount path 중 A:\ ~ Z:\ 형태의 드라이브 문자 root를 찾은 뒤, 해당 volume에 System Volume Information\FsTx directory가 있으면 recovery 후보로 넣습니다.

// VolumeContext::FindFsTxVolumes 요약GetVolumePathNamesForVolumeNameW(volumeGuid, mountPaths, ...);for (WCHAR *i = mountPaths; *i; i += wcslen(i) + 1) {    if (wcslen(i) == 3 && i[1] == L':' && i[2] == L'\\') {        driveLetter = *i;        break;    }}if (!driveLetter) continue;wcscat_s(path, MAX_PATH, L"System Volume Information\\FsTx");DWORD attrs = GetFileAttributesW(path);if (attrs == INVALID_FILE_ATTRIBUTES || !(attrs & FILE_ATTRIBUTE_DIRECTORY))    continue;candidates.push_back(volume);

즉 이 함수는 드라이브 문자와 System Volume Information\FsTx directory의 존재를 기준으로 recovery 대상을 고릅니다. 외부 USB가 같은 구조를 가지면 recovery 후보에 들어가고, 이후 AutoFsTxSession::RunSession은 해당 volume의 session을 찾아 FsTxPerformRecovery(handle, 0, 60000)으로 replay를 시작합니다.

// AutoFsTxSession::RunSession 내부, 각 후보에 대한 recovery 처리messageContext = (AutoFsTxSession *)((char *)session + 96);if (recoveryStatus >= 0) {    FsTxMessageContext::OutputMessage(messageContext, 2u, 0x3F4u, sessionIndex);    v50 = 1;} else {    FsTxMessageContext::OutputMessage(messageContext, 8u, 0x3F5u, sessionIndex, recoveryStatus);    v50 = 0;}*(_BYTE *)(fsTxSession + 98) = v50;FsTxSession::CloseSession((FsTxSession *)fsTxSession, closeReason);// 실제 replay 호출 지점 (동적 로드된 FsTx.dll의 export)pfnFsTxPerformRecovery = (int64 (*)(int64, QWORD, int64))g_FsTxPerformRecovery;FsTxVolumes = pfnFsTxPerformRecovery(sessionHandle, 0, 60000);

autofstx.exe는 FsTx.dll이 수행한 작업을 직접 처리하지 않고, 성공과 실패 결과값을 받아 로그를 남깁니다. winpeshl.ini 삭제는 FsTx.dll의 replay 단계에서 발생합니다.

이제 실제 코드에서 USB volume이 recovery candidate로 선택되는 지점과, rollback이 LinkPath를 처리하는 지점을 확인해보겠습니다.

Root Cause 코드

① VolumeContext::FindFsTxVolumes - 신뢰 안 되는 USB를 복구 후보로 수용

BaseAddress = FindFirstVolumeW(Str);// ← 모든 볼륨 순회 (fixed/removable/USB 구분 없음)// 드라이브문자 root(X:\) 있나? 확인if ( v20 == 3 && i[1] == 58 /* ':' */ && i[2] == 92 /* '\' */ && (letter a-z/A-Z) )    v17 = *i;                              // 드라이브문자 확보// 유일한 자격 검사: "<드라이브>:\System Volume Information\FsTx" 폴더가 존재하나?wcscat_s(Str, 0x104u, L"System Volume Information\\FsTx");FileAttributesW = GetFileAttributesW(Str);if ( FileAttributesW == -1 || (FileAttributesW & 0x10) == 0 )    v7 = 0;                                // 폴더 없으면 탈락LABEL_54:    v23 = AutoChkMalloc(0x48u);            // ★ 여기서 볼륨이 "복구 후보"로 채택됨    ...    v24[66] = v7;                          // v7(+0x42) = "복구 대상 여부" → RunSession이 이걸로 recover 결정

앞서 소개하였듯, 드라이브 문자와 System Volume Information\FsTx directory가 있으면 이 volume은 recovery 후보로 처리되는 것을 알 수 있습니다.

② PerformOperationRollbackRecovery (op==5) - 교차볼륨 winpeshl.ini 삭제

if ( opType == 5 )   // HARDLINK 생성을 롤백한다.{    TempRootPath = (wchar_t *)GetTempRootPath(recoveryCtx, linkPath, linkPath);    v30 = TempRootPath;    if ( TempRootPath )    {        v43 = AddPathToPathSet((PRTL_DYNAMIC_HASH_TABLE)(recoveryCtx + 2152), TempRootPath);        RtlNtStatusToDosError(v43);    }    HIDWORD(v115) = 0;    File = (HANDLE)DoCreateFile(recoveryCtx, 0, (_DWORD)Name, (unsigned int)&v135, *(_DWORD *)(opRecord + 12) & 8);    // ↑ Name(= 레코드 path[1] = \??\X:\Windows\System32\winpeshl.ini)을    //   절대 NT 경로로 그냥 연다. 이 경로가 어느 볼륨인지, 이 트랜잭션의    //   소스 볼륨과 같은지 확인하는 코드가 여기 없다.    if ( File != (HANDLE)-1LL || (LastWin32Error = RtlGetLastWin32Error()) != 0 )    {        v44 = LastWin32Error;        if ( LastWin32Error == 2 ) // 링크 없음 → 스킵        {            LastWin32Error = 0;            goto LABEL_225;        }        if ( !LastWin32Error )        {            dispositionFlags = 17;            // 0x11 = DELETE | POSIX - 취약: 교차볼륨 무검증 삭제            SetFileInformationByHandle(File);            // 그대로 POSIX 삭제            goto LABEL_225;        }    }    else    {        LastWin32Error = 6;        v44 = 6;    }    // open 실패 로그    LODWORD(v110) = 10506;    if ( swprintf_s(           v21,           0x800u,           L"%s:%u (Error 0x%X) - Rollback recovery(HARDLINK): Failed to open hard link '%s' for deletion, to reve"            "rt the operation",           L"onecore\\base\\fs\\fstxlib\\dll\\fstxlib.c",           v110,           v44,           Name) < 0 )      wcscpy_s(v21, 0x800u, L"???");

문제는 DoCreateFile()이 record의 Name을 절대 NT path로 그대로 열고, 그 파일이 실제로 이 transaction이 만들었던 link인지 다시 확인하지 않는다는 점입니다. USB에서 읽은 transaction record가 X:\Windows\System32\winpeshl.ini를 LinkPath로 지정하면, FsTx.dll은 source USB volume과 무관한 이 기존 파일도 rollback으로 되돌려야 할 link로 취급합니다. 이후 dispositionFlags = 0x11이 적용되면 해당 path의 파일은 POSIX delete로 제거됩니다.

4.5 재현 결과

먼저 USB에 E:에 FsTx artifact를 배치하였습니다. 정상 부팅에서는 WinRE 복구 UI가 표시될텐데, USB 주입 후 부팅을 했을 때의 재현 결과를 확인해봅시다.

의도한 FsTx artifact를 배치한 USB를 연결하고 WinRE로 부팅하면 정상 복구 UI 대신 X:\Windows\System32\cmd.exe가 표시됩니다. winpeshl.exe와 winpeshl.log같은 파일들은 남아있는데, 같은 디렉토리에 있어야 할 X:\Windows\System32\winpeshl.ini를 찾지 못하는 것으로 보아 rollback으로 삭제된 것으로 볼 수 있습니다.

winpeshl.log를 확인해보면 X:\Windows\System32\cmd.exe /K startnet.cmd를 실행했다는 로그도 확인할 수 있습니다. cmd.exe fallback이 실행되었네요.

winre_access_proof.txt에 WinRE_ACCESS_PROOF와 timestamp가 기록되었고, WinRE 세션에서 만든 마커파일에 파일 쓰기가 잘 이뤄진 것을 볼 수 있습니다!

마치며

이번 글에서는 평소에는 지나치기 쉬운 WinRE의 부팅 과정과 recovery code를 직접 따라가 봤는데요. 이 글을 읽으신 여러분들이라면 이제 우연히 Windows 복구 모드에 들어가더라도 파란 복구 화면 뒤에는 일반 Windows와 별도로 부팅된 WinRE가 복구 기능을 준비하고 실행하고 있구나~ 하고 떠올리실 수 있을 것 같습니다. 😁

WinRE 시리즈, 재밌으셨나요? 다음 글에서는 WinRE보다 한 단계 앞선 Boot Manager로 돌아가, BitPixie를 살펴보겠습니다. 구버전의 서명된 Boot Manager가 왜 다시 실행될 수 있었는지와, 그 뒤 PXE 전환 과정에서 어떤 일이 일어나는지도 함께 알아보겠습니다! 많은 기대 부탁드립니다!

Reference

  1. Alon Leviev, Netanel Ben Simon, “BitUnlocker: Leveraging Windows Recovery to Extract BitLocker Secrets,” Microsoft Security Blog, August 13, 2025.

    https://techcommunity.microsoft.com/blog/microsoft-security-blog/bitunlocker-leveraging-windows-recovery-to-extract-bitlocker-secrets/4442806

  2. Nightmare-Eclipse, “YellowKey: BitLocker Bypass Vulnerability,” GitHub, 2026. (Archived copy)

    https://github.com/meltingscales/YellowKey

  3. Microsoft Security Response Center, “CVE-2026-45585: Windows BitLocker Security Feature Bypass Vulnerability,” Microsoft Security Update Guide, 2026.

    https://msrc.microsoft.com/update-guide/vulnerability/CVE-2026-45585

  4. Microsoft, “WinPE: Create Apps,” Microsoft Learn.

    https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-hardware/manufacture/desktop/winpe-create-apps

item.title: [하루한줄] CVE-2026-110264 : GitLab의 Integer Overflow로 인한 Remote Code Execution
item.content:encoded:
URL

  • https://docs.gitlab.com/releases/patches/patch-release-gitlab-19-5-1-released/

Target

  • GitLab CE/EE 7.0 ~ 18.11.12
  • GitLab CE/EE 19.0.x < 19.0.10
  • GitLab CE/EE 19.1.x < 19.1.9
  • GitLab CE/EE 19.2.x < 19.2.9
  • GitLab CE/EE 19.3.x < 19.3.6
  • GitLab CE/EE 19.4.x < 19.4.3
  • GitLab CE/EE 19.5.x < 19.5.1

Explain

CVE-2026-110264는 GitLab에서 사용하는 Ruby 정규표현식 엔진 Onigmo의 Integer Overflow 취약점입니다.
정규표현식의 반복 구문에 부여되는 ID가 16비트 정수 범위를 초과하면서 잘못된 값으로 저장되고, 이를 배열 인덱스로 사용하는 과정에서 Out-of-bounds Write가 발생합니다.

Background

GitLab은 org-ruby 라이브러리를 사용하여 .org 문서를 렌더링합니다. .org 문서에서는 #+TODO: 를 통해 사용자 지정 TODO 키워드를 정의할 수 있습니다.

org-ruby의 headline.rb에는 다음과 같이 키워드를 정규표현식으로 처리하는 코드가 존재합니다.

@headline_text.sub!(Regexp.new("^#{@keyword}\s*"), "")

이때 @keyword를 이스케이프하지 않고 Regexp.new() 에 전달하므로, 키워드에 포함된 정규표현식 문법이 그대로 해석됩니다.

공개 프로젝트에 공격자가 제어하는 .org 파일이 존재하고 GitLab이 이를 렌더링하면, 별도의 인증 없이 취약한 정규표현식 처리 과정에 도달할 수 있습니다.

Root Cause

Onigmo는 정규표현식의 반복 구문마다 ID를 부여합니다. ID는 int로 관리되지만, 컴파일된 명령에 저장할 때는 short int인 MemNumType으로 변환됩니다.

// regint.htypedef short int MemNumType;// regcomp.c - add_mem_num()MemNumType n = (MemNumType )num;BBUF_ADD(reg, &n, SIZE_MEMNUM);

16비트 signed short 환경에서는 ID가 32,767을 초과하면 음수로 변환될 수 있습니다. 그러나 취약한 버전에는 이 값의 범위를 검사하는 코드가 존재하지 않습니다.

이후 정규표현식을 실행할 때 regexec.c 의 OP_REPEAT 에서 저장된 ID를 읽어 배열 인덱스로 사용합니다.

CASE(OP_REPEAT)  MOP_IN(OP_REPEAT);  {GET_MEMNUM_INC(mem, p);    /* mem: OP_REPEAT ID */GET_RELADDR_INC(addr, p);STACK_ENSURE(1);repeat_stk[mem] = GET_STACK_INDEX(stk);STACK_PUSH_REPEAT(mem, p);if (reg->repeat_range[mem].lower == 0) {  CHECK_MATCH_CACHE;  STACK_PUSH_ALT(p + addr, s, sprev, pkeep);}  }

repeat_stk는 OnigStackIndex 타입의 배열로, 각 반복 구문(OP_REPEAT)이 백트래킹 스택의 어느 위치까지 진행되었는지를 저장합니다.
이 배열은 원래 alloca()로 스레드 스택에 할당되지만, 정규표현식의 그룹 수가 MAX_PTR_NUM을 초과하면 스택 오버플로를 피하기 위해 xmalloc()으로 힙에 할당됩니다.

여기서 mem이 음수가 되면 repeat_stk 의 시작 주소보다 앞쪽에 값이 기록되어 OOB Write가 발생합니다.

정규표현식을 컴파일하면서 반복 ID가 잘못 저장되고, 매칭 과정에서 해당 ID를 배열 인덱스로 사용하면서 메모리 손상이 발생합니다.

PoC

공개 PoC 저장소에서는 GitLab CE 19.3.1을 대상으로 .org 파일을 렌더링할 때 발생하는 처리 지연과 Timeout::Error를 확인했습니다.

#+TODO: 키워드에 반복되는 정규표현식 구문을 포함시킵니다. 다음은 반복 패턴을 생성하는 코드 일부입니다.

UNIT_LOUD = "[[:word:]]*"REPEATS_DEFAULT = 35000def build_keyword(repeats=REPEATS_DEFAULT, unit=UNIT_LOUD):    return unit * repeats

생성한 키워드를 포함한 .org 문서를 GitLab에서 렌더링하여 정상 문서 응답 시간을 비교하였고, 지연된 렌더링 시간이 확인되었습니다.

그리고, 서버의 exceptions_json.log 에서도 .org 렌더링 과정에서 발생한 Timeout::Error가 확인되었습니다.

Patch

Ruby에서는 2026년 4월 PR #16801을 통해 반복 ID과 널 체크 ID의 범위를 검사하는 코드를 추가했습니다. regcomp.c의 compile_range_repeat_node()에 추가된 코드는 다음과 같습니다.

@@ -703,6 +704,7 @@ compile_range_repeat_node(QtfrNode* qn, int target_len, int empty_info,  if (r) return r;  r = add_mem_num(reg, num_repeat); /* OP_REPEAT ID */  reg->num_repeat++;+ if ((MemNumType)reg->num_repeat <= 0) return ONIGERR_TOO_MANY_RANGE_REPEAT;  if (r) return r;  r = add_rel_addr(reg, target_len + SIZE_OP_REPEAT_INC);  if (r) return r;

MemNumType으로 변환한 값이 0 이하가 되면 오류를 반환하고 컴파일을 중단합니다. num_null_check에도 동일한 검사가 추가되었으며, 정규표현식 컴파일 시 RegexpError가 발생하도록 수정되었습니다.

해당 수정은 당시 Ruby 메인 브랜치에만 적용되어 GitLab에서 사용하던 Ruby 3.3, 3.4, 4.0에는 포함되지 않았습니다.

이후 GitLab은 해당 패치를 번들 Ruby에 백포트하고, 2026년 10월 21일 다음 버전의 보안 업데이트를 배포했습니다.

  • GitLab CE/EE: 18.11.13, 19.0.10, 19.1.9, 19.2.9, 19.3.6, 19.4.3, 19.5.1
  • Ruby: 3.3.13, 3.4.12, 4.0.9

GitLab은 Ruby 3.3, 3.4, 4.0에 각각 적용할 패치 파일을 추가했으며, config/software/ruby.rb에서 해당 패치를 적용하도록 변경했습니다.

한편 org-ruby에서도 PR #112를 통해 사용자 지정 TODO 키워드에 Regexp.escape()를 적용하도록 수정했습니다.

@@ -97,7 +97,7 @@ def parse_keywords      words = @headline_text.split      if words.length > 0 && words[0] =~ re then        @keyword = words[0]-       @headline_text.sub!(Regexp.new("^#{@keyword}\s*"), "")+       @headline_text.sub!(Regexp.new("^#{Regexp.escape(@keyword)}\s*"), "")      end    end  end

이 수정은 TODO 키워드에 포함된 정규표현식 특수문자를 일반 문자열로 처리하도록 합니다. GitLab의 Ruby 백포트와는 별도로 진행된 org-ruby의 수정입니다.

Reference

  • https://docs.gitlab.com/releases/patches/patch-release-gitlab-19-5-1-released/
  • https://github.com/ruby/ruby/blob/v3_4_11/regint.h
  • https://github.com/ruby/ruby/blob/v3_4_11/regcomp.c
  • https://github.com/ruby/ruby/blob/v3_4_11/regexec.c
  • https://github.com/ruby/ruby/commit/493d26dcdea8b2f0ac5d28e057b401bc809e7fae
  • https://github.com/wallyqs/org-ruby/commit/aa961a6
  • https://github.com/wallyqs/org-ruby/pull/112
  • https://github.com/gitlabhq/omnibus-gitlab/commit/73cec6d8013db9a70175904fd24c9342fa63454a
  • https://github.com/googlesky/CVE-2026-110264

item.title: [Lone Wolves] Analyzing an Android Auto Dongle - Part 1
item.description:
0. Intro

Hel
item.content:encoded:
0. Intro

Hello! This is t0be. Today, I’m back with the next post following the “Lone Wolves” project that gongjae posted earlier! 🐺

Before we begin, though, there’s one thing I’d like to mention. Although we’re working on this project together as a team, each of us has different interests, so it feels like we’re a team, but also not quite a team. Because of this, gongjae’s macOS research article and this post cover completely different topics.

Since I focus on automotive security, my mind naturally went to the vehicle itself or its internal Electronic Control Units (ECUs) at first. Then, a thought suddenly crossed my mind: “What if I look into peripherals instead of the vehicle itself… wouldn’t they be vulnerable?”

While searching for various candidates, a product caught my eye: a wireless Android Auto / CarPlay dongle.

In fact, this was a product I had saved in my shopping cart a while ago because I wanted to use Android Auto wirelessly in my car. Just plug it into the vehicle, pair it with your smartphone, and you’re done! It has quite impressive capabilities for its small size, but I always wondered how secure it actually was.

After all, a third-party device handling Bluetooth, Wi-Fi, and USB simultaneously is introduced right between the vehicle and the smartphone. On top of that, this device processes data displayed on the car’s screen and handles mirroring sessions from the smartphone. What a appetizing target to analyze!

The product I analyzed this time is an Ottocast CP88-M series wireless mirroring dongle sold under the Anniver brand. I bought it directly on Coupang. I physically opened the device, observed its USB communications, obtained its OTA firmware and SPI flash, reverse-engineered it, and verified a few security issues firsthand.

My original plan was simply: “Let’s quickly crack open the firmware and take a look!” However, I ended up diving into everything from RISC-V extended instructions to firmware update structures. Oh dear, I crossed the point of no return 😇

In this article, I will focus on how this dongle works, how I acquired and analyzed the firmware, what I actually verified, and what remains a hypothesis at this stage.

Actually, I couldn’t be the only one who has analyzed a product like this, right? When I started analyzing, I looked for materials covering similar dongles, and sec1.dk’s Reverse Engineering a Wireless CarPlay Adapter — Full Journey caught my attention. It was a comprehensive article covering everything from acquiring firmware to OTA, hardware analysis, flash recovery, and getting a root shell. Thanks to that, I didn’t have to start from scratch and redo all the trial and error without any clues.

Fortunately, our work didn’t overlap completely, which is why I’m able to share this research. The target in the referenced article was based on the Allwinner V851S3 (ARM), while the product I bought turned out to be based on the V821 (RISC-V). Furthermore, even the firmware file structures differed slightly. Therefore, I decided to verify actual behavior and potential vulnerabilities directly on my device.

Scope of Analysis: Tested without an actual vehicle using a CP88-M dongle owned by the researcher and a Pixel 10a. No attacks were performed on vehicle head units, CAN networks, or vehicle control functions.

1. How to work?

1-1. What exactly does an Android Auto dongle do?

First, let me clarify something that confused me at the beginning. Looking at the name alone, doesn’t it feel like just plugging in this dongle would magically add Android Auto functionality to a vehicle that doesn’t support Android Auto at all?

However, the CP88-M analyzed here is essentially an adapter that converts a vehicle’s factory-supported wired CarPlay or Android Auto into a wireless connection. If the vehicle itself does not support these functions natively, plugging in the dongle alone won’t enable them. The manufacturer’s product description also assumes existing wired functionality. I heard there are products that enable Android Auto on unsupported vehicles, but due to the limits of my searching skills, I couldn’t find one.

Looking at the operational principle, it’s surprisingly intuitive:

                 Bluetooth / Wi-Fi                USB┌──────────────┐      Wireless Conn.   ┌───────────────────┐     Wired Conn.   ┌────────────────┐│   Smartphone │ <-----------------> │ CP88-M Dongle     │ <-------------> │ Car Head Unit  ││ Android / iOS│                     │ Linux + BT + Wi-Fi│                   │ (Wired AA/CP)  │└──────────────┘                     └───────────────────┘                   └────────────────┘    Wireless Android Auto/CarPlay Receiver     Session Processing & Relay      Behaves like Wired Phone

The dongle acts like a car providing wireless Android Auto/CarPlay to the smartphone, while acting like a smartphone plugged into USB to the car’s head unit. It takes wirelessly received data and passes it to the wired side, and forwards user input or control data from the vehicle back in the opposite direction.

In other words, this product is not a simple USB cable adapter. It can be viewed as a small embedded bridge equipped with its own OS and communication stack to process protocols between two devices.

So, what happens if this device, sitting right in the middle where both devices trust each other, is compromised by an attacker?

Of course, being in the middle doesn’t mean all traffic is automatically decrypted or that arbitrary commands can be executed. That depends on the authentication, encryption, and session state of the actual protocol. However, from an attacker’s perspective, it certainly looks like a juicy device.

1-2. A $30 iPhone?

First, I connected the dongle to my PC and checked the USB descriptor. But I was surprised because no matter how hard I looked, I couldn’t see anything that looked like a dongle.

Bus 003 Device 006: ID 05ac:12a8 Apple, Inc. iPhone  idVendor           0x05ac Apple, Inc.  idProduct          0x12a8 iPhone  iManufacturer           Apple Inc.  iProduct                iPhone  bNumConfigurations      4

I connected an Android Auto dongle, but it reported that an Apple iPhone was connected. Whew~ If I were using an iPhone instead of a Galaxy, I almost wouldn’t have found it!

At first, I thought another USB device was captured, but even after disconnecting everything except the dongle, the same values appeared. The dongle was advertising its USB descriptor as an iPhone, rather than an actual iPhone.

USB ConfigurationFeature Identified in Descriptor
Configuration 1PTP (Picture Transfer Protocol)
Configuration 2iPod / iAP-related Interface
Configuration 3Apple Mobile Device, USB Multiplexor
Configuration 4Apple Mobile Device + USB Ethernet

CarPlay uses a USB interface alongside an IP-based session. Therefore, to make it appear as if a wired iPhone is connected to the head unit, it needs to provide interfaces like these.

Initially, only Configuration 1 was selected properly, while Configurations 2–4 failed. I wondered, “Is it just impersonating the descriptor without actual functionality?” But once the smartphone was paired and I checked again, the other Configurations became active.

When I set the Pixel and dongle to Android Auto mode, the USB device side of the dongle connected to the PC was now displayed as 2717:ff40 with the product name CAR2. Sending an AOA (Android Open Accessory) control request caused the USB device to re-enumerate, changing its ID to 18d1:2d00. Originally, 18d1:2d00 is defined in the Android AOA documentation as the ID for accessory mode on Android devices. Here, the dongle is imitating that role on the USB port side connecting to the car. First pretending to be an iPhone, and now an Android… it’s quite busy.

AOA_GET_PROTOCOL (Request 51)  -> Version 2AOA_SEND_IDENT   (Request 52)  -> Send Identification StringAOA_START        (Request 53)  -> Switch to Accessory ModeUSB ID Change: 2717:ff40  ->  18d1:2d00

In short, this product identifies itself as different USB devices in CarPlay and Android Auto modes. As a side note, the USB ID change mentioned above was observed on the dongle connected to the PC, not a case where the Pixel was connected via USB and re-enumerated. Furthermore, confirming the transition to AOA mode does not mean the entire Android Auto session is complete. Although I succeeded in sending the actual AA version request via Bulk OUT, I couldn’t verify responses or TLS sessions because a stack acting as the head unit wasn’t fully set up. I’m trying to borrow a car from people around me, but it’s not easy.

1-3. Why are both Bluetooth and Wi-Fi required?

Even though it’s called wireless mirroring, screen data isn’t transmitted entirely over Bluetooth. Typically, Bluetooth handles device discovery, pairing, and initial connection setup, while high-bandwidth mirroring data utilizes the Wi-Fi/IP path.

I found elements corresponding to this structure in this dongle as well.

ComponentConfirmed Role
btappHandles Bluetooth connection, uses /dev/ttyS1
hostapdOperates 5GHz Wi-Fi AP
wpa_supplicantConfigures Wi-Fi Direct (P2P)
udhcpdAssigns IP addresses to connected devices
mdnsdAdvertises network services
rcpserviceCarPlay session and network communication
raaserviceService binary for Android Auto mode

In practice, the dongle advertised a Wi-Fi AP named CAR2-2F7D, with IP assignments being 192.168.1.101 for the dongle and 192.168.1.102 for the connected Pixel. A Wi-Fi Direct group was also confirmed on the same hardware.

In the Pixel logs, I could observe a flow initiating an RFCOMM connection to a previously registered device and attempting to connect to Wi-Fi using saved credentials. This means automatic reconnection happens without requiring fresh pairing every time. While convenient from a usability perspective, from an attacker’s perspective, it implies that an accessory trusted once will continue to be trusted later. This raised my curiosity regarding how much impact compromising such a device could have on the phone or vehicle side.

Of course, up to this point, these are all normal functionalities. The fact that automatic reconnection occurs doesn’t automatically mean pairing bypasses or data leaks are immediately possible.

2. Firmware Acquisition

Now let’s take a proper look inside. This analysis progressed from USB to wireless network, OTA, flash dump, and binary reverse engineering.

Looking at prior research, update servers and other interfaces could serve as good starting points, but I naturally didn’t expect my device to share the exact same addresses, partitions, or validation logic. Therefore, I decided to proceed step-by-step using values measured directly from my device.

2-1. Firmware Extraction

At first, I wondered if I should teardown the hardware and read the SPI flash right away, as is typical in embedded analysis. While I was naturally preparing my CH341A, I asked my best friend ChatGPT to check it out. After connecting to the dongle’s Wi-Fi, navigating to http://192.168.1.101 brought up the settings page, and it began analyzing the features on its own. (Yay!)

The report generated by ChatGPT showed features like device info, settings modification, and firmware updates on the web UI. Naturally, what interested me most was the Firmware Update—since I might be able to obtain the firmware without tearing down the hardware!

Here, sec1.dk’s analysis post was very helpful. In that post, the author followed the OTA path on the settings page of a similar product to obtain official firmware, outlining a structure where an MD5 string is prepended to the package, followed by a CPIO archive for SWUpdate. Instead of blindly copying those paths, I first checked what URLs my dongle’s web page generated.

Examining cpbox.js and index.html used by the page revealed the update flow:

[Management Page]    |    | 1. Check current version (?id=host)    v[Request OTA Version Info]    |    | 2. Check build/release info in version.json    v[Download Firmware Image]    |    | 3. Download update.img    v[Dongle's Upload CGI]    |    | 4. Save to /tmp/update.img & process update    v[SWUpdate]

The device version string was 26061510.5140.2, and the update management code used 5140 (corresponding to the model/project line) to construct the OTA object path. At the time of testing, firmware images and version information could be downloaded without authentication from known object paths on the vendor’s OTA repository. It wasn’t that the entire repository directory listing was exposed, but rather that known update object paths were directly accessible.

Obtaining the firmware made me think everything was solved. However, inspecting the file header brought up another problem.

2-2. Encrypted Firmware

Some older images from the same product family had the following structure:

<MD5 Checksum>  update.swu070702...                 # CPIO (newc + CRC)  ├── sw-description      # Update Metadata  ├── kernel              # Kernel Image  └── rootfs              # Root Filesystem

Here, sw-description is a manifest determining which files SWUpdate installs where. Prior research had already pointed out that confusing 070701 (newc) with 070702 (newc with CRC) causes SWUpdate to reject the package. Thanks to that insight, when handling the package, I checked which CPIO format was used and at which offset in the file the header started.

Indeed, the simple CPIO parser I initially wrote stopped right after reading the first member. Because of the leading MD5 string, the archive start offset wasn’t zero, but alignment calculations were made relative to the beginning of the file. Fixing the alignment reference to the CPIO start offset allowed sw-description, kernel, and rootfs to be read sequentially.

However, in newer model lines closer to my target, normal CPIO headers were still not immediately visible. At first, I wondered if it was an encrypted image. Asking ChatGPT didn’t yield a full recovery either. Downloading the firmware was the easy part…

However, while comparing images across various builds, I noticed something strange. Although they were different files, bytes in certain sections were identical. This pattern was hard to explain if independent nonces/IVs were used for encryption per image.

I considered the possibility of a repeating short XOR key and searched for a period, but that wasn’t it either. Hoping to at least recover the header, I downloaded older firmware versions as a last resort… and fortunately, older firmware left on the vendor’s server was in plaintext! I could use the CPIO structure and known parts of sw-description identified earlier as known plaintext.

# Compare identical offsets exclusively within sections where plaintext is availablekeystream = bytes(c ^ p for c, p in zip(encrypted_bytes, known_plaintext_bytes))candidate_plaintext = bytes(c ^ k for c, k in zip(other_encrypted_bytes, keystream))

Applying the keystream recovered from identical positions to images of other models revealed structurally valid sw-description contents. Text encrypted in other models such as 5110/5130 was restored, and model-specific project names were verified normally. By confirming a shared XOR keystream in sections where known plaintext was obtained, it was possible to apply it to subsequent firmwares. Of course, I couldn’t perfectly decrypt every single byte of the latest image. Nevertheless, it clearly demonstrated that XOR-based OTA obfuscation fails to properly protect firmware confidentiality. It was a prime example showing why independent encryption per image is necessary. At this point, one wonders if they even intended to hide it properly.

2-3. Not Satisfied! Bring On the Flash ROM~!

What I got from OTA was primarily the files targeted for updates. To analyze the full boot process and the base rootfs, I needed the full flash. Originally, I planned to clip onto the SPI NOR chip and read it, but after reading the aforementioned sec1.dk article describing a recovery process using Allwinner FEL (USB download mode of the BootROM), I changed my plan.

I disassembled it immediately and decided to check the interfaces supported by the device first before attempting soldering or SPI clips.

Using tweezers on the relevant pads, I attempted to trigger mode switching. Initially, instead of the expected FEL device, the USB ID changed to 0525:a4a7. I initially noted this in my project notes as A2A Debug Mode, but upon looking it up, I found this ID is used as the CDC ACM example for USB Gadget Serial in the Linux Kernel Documentation. Still, there was no concrete evidence that a debug console actually opened. At any rate, it was clearly not FEL, so I retried several times. Finally, the ID changed to 1f3a:efe8, and xfel recognized it as a V821.

FEL USB enumeration : 1f3a:efe8xfel version         : AWUSBFEX ID=0x00188200 (V821)SPI NOR flash        : 16,777,216 bytes (16 MiB)

Looking solely at the TC397 marking on the chip surface, Infineon AURIX/TriCore first came to mind. However, the ID read via USB FEL and the extracted kernel/executables pointed to an Allwinner V821-based RISC-V platform. Judging the SoC purely by chip markings would have led me down the wrong path entirely. As for why it has that marking… I honestly don’t know either.

To ensure the integrity of the extracted firmware, I read the entire binary three separate times and verified that all SHA-256 hashes matched before proceeding with analysis. Having a recoverable original backup made me feel much more at ease, as an incorrect modification could render the device unbootable. With this, all foundational preparation for vulnerability analysis and testing was complete.

Analyzing the dump with binwalk and unsquashfs produced the following results:

Flash OffsetIdentified Component
0x000000Boot Region (SPL/boot0)
0x060000Kernel Boot Image
0x370000Kernel Boot Image Copy
0x680000SquashFS rootfs
0xB00000SquashFS customer
Around 0xED0050JFFS2 Writable Data

Inside the filesystem, alongside Linux kernel 5.4.220, BusyBox, and musl libc, were device boot scripts, Wi-Fi configurations, a web server, and update utilities. It feels like analyzing a standard embedded Linux device inside this tiny gadget. I expected nothing much, but it was packed quite densely.

As a side note, while organizing this article, I also cross-referenced lvalen91’s C2Air V821 platform analysis notes. Other products in those notes match in several configurations: V821, 16MB SPI NOR, Linux 5.4.220, rootfs at 0x680000 / customer at 0xB00000. While this hints at a common platform across product lines, the offsets and SoC identification above are strictly based on the flash dumps and FEL results I measured directly.

3. Reverse Engineering

Now that we have the firmware, it’s time to analyze the binaries.

However, as mentioned earlier… yes, the binaries are RISC-V 32-bit ELFs. Having prior research available made me think it would be a breeze, but when running some executables in qemu-riscv32, an Illegal instruction occurred, and Ghidra displayed unfamiliar code in the middle of functions.

In the past, one would have to look up each instruction manually and fix alignment, but nowadays this isn’t much of a problem.

After feeding it to ChatGPT, I confirmed that Andes vendor extension instructions were being used. If Ghidra fails to interpret these properly, it doesn’t just result in messy pseudocode—string references disappear, branch targets break, and ultimately entire function execution flows get truncated. Of course, just saying “it solved it all” is too result-oriented, so let’s look through the issues together one by one.

Among the analysis targets, about 14.9% of .text in /sbin/update and about 12.3% in index.cgi consisted of these custom opcodes. Left as is, it would be impossible to follow critical request-handling logic properly.

3-1. ADDIGP

While strings in index.cgi could be found in Ghidra, cross-references (xrefs) to those strings were not connected properly. Tracing the cause showed that custom-0 series instructions mapped to Andes ADDIGP, which calculates global addresses.

ADDIGP is used to reference data relative to the Global Pointer (gp). When Ghidra treats this like an unknown function call, it fails to resolve addresses calculated via gp, severing string xrefs.

Initially, I guessed conventional gp values, but results were off by several bytes. What made it even more frustrating was that in dense string regions, wrong addresses still looked like plausible strings. I was so happy thinking I got it right, only to realize I was wrong upon second look.

So I tracked the auipc/addi combination in the ELF initialization code to determine the exact gp value and statistically verified if addresses landed cleanly within actual data sections. As a result, I was able to restore many lost string references in Ghidra.

For example, in index.cgi, recalculating relative to gp=0x17800 resulted in 418 out of 510 candidates (approx. 82%) matching exact starting positions of valid strings. Unlike guessing blindly based on .sdata + 0x800, I could now trace which strings index.cgi was actually referencing.

3-2. BEQC/BNEC

Next was an issue with the command dispatcher in rcpservice. Reading it like standard RISC-V instructions resulted in a series of incomprehensible branches, but inspecting surrounding code revealed a switch structure choosing handlers based on command IDs.

The decisive clues here were the numbers appearing as comparison values:

1, 2, 3, 5, 11, 12, 13, 16

Fields that looked like register numbers turned out to be individual command codes! Reinterpreting instruction bits [24:20] as immediate comparison values (cimm) and applying standard RISC-V B-type formatting for branch offsets caused eight branches to lead to valid handler starting addresses.

custom-2 / funct3=5 -> BEQC (Branch if Register == Constant)custom-2 / funct3=7 -> BNEC (Branch if Register != Constant)Comparison Immediate: instruction[24:20]Branch Displacement : RISC-V B-type immediate

Interpreting branch displacements in various ways revealed that 97.5% using standard B-type displacement landed on valid instruction starting points. Other candidates yielded 60–75%, and a simple even-address baseline yielded 63.9%, showing a significant difference. In particular, the 8 commands in rcpservice led precisely to 8 distinct handler starting addresses. For instance, beqc s10, 1 jumps to 0x1c5c0, and beqc s10, 11 jumps to 0x1c608. At this point, I was confident in the decoding logic.

When loading into Ghidra, I patched these branches to standard beq instructions in an analysis copy (rather than the original executable) to reconstruct the Control Flow Graph (CFG). However, there is an important limitation: while branch destinations were preserved, the semantic meaning of comparison conditions wasn’t fully maintained. Therefore, pseudocode obtained this way serves as reference material to follow handler structure, and detailed condition evaluations must be cross-checked against original instructions.

Analyzing an Android Auto dongle only to end up reconstructing RISC-V instruction encodings was quite exhausting… ㅠㅠ

3-3. Runtime Binary Extraction

Following the boot script lyLink.sh, I found that certain services were not placed as ordinary files. This was because a vendor container called lylink was extracted into /tmp/app using lypack before services were executed.

init / rcS   └── lyLink.sh         ├── Extract lylink via lypack -> /tmp/app/         ├── CarPlay Path    : rcpservice, lylinkapp, mdnsd ...         └── Android Auto Path: raaservice, mtpservice ...

Looking purely at static files meant missing part of the binaries that actually needed analysis. Furthermore, lypack itself relied on Andes instructions, making it unexecutable in standard qemu-riscv32. I wondered if I had to reverse engineer the entire archive format from scratch, but realized I didn’t need to—the actual physical device already unpacks and uses those files during boot!

Once again, I got a hint from prior research. sec1.dk modified the boot script in customer and reflashed via the recovery interface to build an analysis root shell. Referencing the core idea—‘full flash backup → target modification of customer section → write/verify read via FEL’—I adapted it to my device environment by adding a diagnostic CGI. This was necessary because the default BusyBox lacked utilities like telnetd or nc, preventing me from running identical commands directly.

Using physical FEL access and backups, I prepared a modified image for research and obtained an analysis shell with uid=0(root) in that environment. After that, all that was left was to retrieve the binaries the device unpacked into /tmp/app at runtime. A hurdle that nearly required full reverse engineering of an archive format was bypassed through runtime observation.

The files acquired here—such as rcpservice, librcarplay.so, and libriap2.so—allowed me to inspect CarPlay-related network services and parsers in greater detail.

4. Conclusion

It definitely started with “Let’s crack open a $30 dongle,” but plugging it into USB showed an iPhone, fetching the firmware hid the headers, and Ghidra showed nothing but a flood of custom2 instructions.

Still, after obtaining the firmware via OTA, reading the flash via FEL, and pushing through roadblocks caused by Andes instructions, I made it through. Having gathered binaries unpacked to /tmp/app at boot, all the materials needed for analysis are finally collected.

So, what’s next in Part 2? The whole point of buying this dongle was to see if there were vulnerabilities. Now it’s time to dive into vulnerability analysis proper. I plan to examine everything step-by-step, from the dongle’s Wi-Fi and Web API to index.cgi upload handling, and /sbin/update alongside SWUpdate firmware update procedures. I’ll also share what was actually possible and where roadblocks occurred. Finally time for the main course. Got to give it a taste!

Note that the root shell obtained in Part 1 was created by physically opening the device and modifying the firmware to build an analysis environment. This doesn’t mean it was popped remotely—that needs to be analyzed separately.

What started as a lightweight project ended up having much more to look into than expected, extending it into Part 2. Thank you for reading this far! See you in the next post!

item.title: [고독한 늑대들] Android Auto dongle을 분석해보자 - Part 1
item.description:

item.title: [하루한줄] CVE-2026-42980 : WMI의 Integer Underflow로 인한 Elevation of Privilege (EoP)
item.content:encoded:
URL

https://msrc.microsoft.com/update-guide/vulnerability/CVE-2026-42980

Target

  • ntoskrnl.exe
  • 2026년 6월 Patch Tuesday 누적 업데이트 이전 빌드

Explain

WMI는 Windows Management Instrumentation의 약어로 ntoskrnl.exe에서 Windows 운영체제, 하드웨어, 프로세스를 조회하고 이벤트 제어 등을 수행하는 기능입니다.

CVE-2026-42980는 여러 개의 WMI 인스턴스 조회 항목을 받아 결과를 하나의 출력 영역에 이어서 WNODE_SINGLE_INSTANCE 구조체에 담아 기록하는 함수 WmipQuerySingleMultiple 에서 발생합니다. 해당 기능은 METHOD_BUFFERED 방식을 사용하므로 I/O manager가 non paged pool에 커널 버퍼인 SystemBuffer를 만들어 이를 통해 입출력을 처리합니다. WmipQuerySingleMultiple 함수에서는 WMI 조회가 끝난 후 결과 크기를 8바이트 단위로 길이를 올림합니다. METHOD_BUFFER 에서의 OutputBuffer는 길이가 정해진 SystemBuffer를 사용합니다. 이때, 결과를 OutputBuffer에 넣을 때 올림한 길이에 대한 범위를 검사하지 않고 남은 OutputBuffer 길이를 계산하면서 Integer Underflow가 발생합니다. 이를 통해 긴 길이의 결과를 반환할 수 있게 되면서, 커널 버퍼인 SystemBuffer에서 non paged pool overflow가 발생합니다.

non paged pool의 WMI SystemBuffer에 인접하게 named pipe객체를 배치하고 해당 취약점을 활용하여 AAR과 AAW를 얻을 수 있습니다. 이를 통해 SYSTEM process의 토큰 값을 덮어 익스플로잇 할 수 있습니다.

Root Cause

CVE-2026-42980은 Integer Underflow로 인해 Heap based buffer overflow가 발생합니다.

① Integer Underflow : Output Buffer Length 계산 검증 미흡

WmipQuerySingleMultiple은 여러 개의 WMI 인스턴스 조회 항목을 받아 결과를 하나의 출력 영역에 이어서 기록합니다. 이때, Output Buffer에 저장하는 값은 조회한 WMI 결과 값의 올림하여 8바이트 정렬 값이지만, 정렬 후 크기는 검증하지 않고 정렬 전 크기만 Output Buffer Length와 비교하여 검증합니다.

WmipQuerySingleMultiple코드는 METHOD_BUFFERED 방식으로 호출된 IOCTL 입니다.

SetExecuteSI = WmipQuerySingleMultiple(                  argIrp,                 1,                 (char *)ioctlSystemBuffer, //output Buffer                 outputBufferLength,                 ioctlSystemBuffer, //input Buffer                 *(_DWORD *)ioctlSystemBuffer,                 0,                 0,                 (unsigned int *)&Handle);

WmipQuerySingleMultiple 함수를 호출 할 때 같은버퍼로 output, input 처리합니다. 이때 전달되는 버퍼가 METHOD_BUFFERED 방식으로 만들어진 커널 버퍼 SystemBuffer가 output과 input을 동시에 처리합니다.

WmipQuerySingleMultiple 함수는 WNODE_SINGLE_INSTANCE 구조체에 결과를 담아 전달합니다.

wnodeCapacity = outputLengthRemain;...memmove(&wnode->VariableData[2], nameCopySource, nameBytesToCopy); resultSize = wnode->WnodeHeader.BufferSize; if ( (int)WmipQuerySetExecuteSI(             currentGuidObject,            Irp,            argMode,            1u,            &wnode->WnodeHeader,            wnodeCapacity, //outputLengthRemain            &resultSize) < 0 ) //[1]  goto LABEL_37;
// WmipQuerySetExcuteSI 함수 내부if ( *returnedSizePtr > argWnodeCapacity ) status = -1073741811;

먼저 사용자가 조회하고자 하는 이름을 빈 wnode 구조체에 작성합니다. 이후 [1]에서 실제 조회를 수행하고 이 때 변수 resultSize에 wnode 구조체에 값을 채운 총 크기가 전달됩니다. 만약, resultSize가 outputLengthRemain 즉, 남은 outputBuffer의 길이보다 작으면 실패합니다.

Provider의 조회 결과가 성공한다면, 조회한 결과 크기를 8바이트 단위로 정렬하여 다음 WNODE의 위치를 계산합니다.
